entries.label: Calls a set of numbers qualitative
entries.description: The student treats a data set made of numbers as qualitative (anecdotal or categorical), reading the numbers as descriptions or group names because they come with a story about people, instead of recognising a set of numbers as quantitative.
entries.signal: Chooses a qualitative option (anecdotal or categorical) for a data set that is a list of numbers.

refutation.text_md: You have treated the numbers as if they were descriptions or names of groups rather than amounts. That is an easy thing to do when the numbers come with a story, such as classmates, shop visitors or a class of learners. You are right that the numbers describe people and things; the slip is letting the story decide.

The first check is on the values themselves. A data set such as the sweets in a packet, $23, 25, 22, 26, 27, 25, 21, 28$, is a set of numbers, and so it must be quantitative. Each number says how many, not which group.

The same holds for heights such as $1.70\text{ m}$ and $1.41\text{ m}$, and for counts such as $3$ questions answered correctly or $14$ SMS messages. Every value is a number, so each of these data sets is quantitative, whoever it was collected from.
Look at the values first. If the data set is a set of numbers, call it quantitative, and only then decide whether it is discrete or continuous.

entries.label: Calls a count continuous
entries.description: The student sees a data set of counts written as whole numbers (messages sent, sweets in a packet, questions answered correctly) and calls it continuous, instead of checking whether each value is a count written as an integer.
entries.signal: Chooses quantitative continuous for a data set of counts written as integers.

refutation.text_md: You were right that this data set is quantitative, because it is made of numbers. The slip comes at the next decision: calling it continuous because the numbers vary a lot or could be many different values, when the question to ask is what each number is.

Take a class asked how many SMS messages they sent yesterday, with answers such as $3$, $0$, $14$ and $30$. Each answer is a count of messages, and a count is written as an integer. There is no answer like $13.5$ messages.

The same is true of the number of sweets in a packet, $23, 25, 22$, or the number of questions answered correctly, $3, 5, 2$. Each value counts whole things and is written as an integer. A set of counts written as integers is discrete, however large or spread out the numbers are.
Next time ask: is each value a count, written as an integer? If so, the data set is quantitative discrete. Keep continuous for values that cannot be represented by integers, such as measurements.

entries.label: Calls a measurement discrete
entries.description: The student sees a data set of measurements written as decimals (heights such as 1.70 m) and calls it discrete, perhaps because it is a short list of separate values, instead of noticing that the values are measurements that cannot be represented by integers.
entries.signal: Chooses quantitative discrete for a data set of measurements written as decimals.

refutation.text_md: You were right that heights are numbers, so the data set is quantitative. The slip is calling it discrete because it is a short list of separate values written down, when what matters is what kind of numbers they are.

A discrete data set is a set of counts written as integers, like the number of sweets in a packet. Now look at heights such as $1.70\text{ m}$, $1.41\text{ m}$ and $1.32\text{ m}$. Nobody counted these. They are measurements, and none of them is an integer.
The length of the list does not decide the type. Six heights or six hundred, they are still measurements that cannot be represented by integers, so the data set is quantitative continuous.
Next time ask: is each value a count written as an integer, or a measurement that cannot be represented by integers? A count is discrete; a measurement like a height is continuous.

flags.text: The only caution supplied (the word data is plural, so say 'the data are') is a point of grammar, not a mathematical error a student makes when classifying data, so no entry rests on it. I kept the wording of the refutations compatible with it by saying 'data set' where a singular subject was needed and 'data are' only where data stands alone.

No wrong turns from an independent re-solve were supplied (the sources file holds only the one caution). All three entries therefore rest on the deliberately written wrong options and on the canonical solutions' own method.

The evidence does not define 'qualitative', 'anecdotal' or 'categorical', so the qualitative entry deliberately does not define them or say how they differ. It argues only from the book's stated step that a set of numbers must be quantitative. Please check that the book does not draw a distinction between anecdotal and categorical that would deserve its own entry.

The words 'measurement' and 'written as an integer / real number' come from the objective's description. The canonical solutions themselves say 'a count', 'represented by integers', 'cannot be represented by integers' and 'a set of numbers'. I used the solutions' wording for the test and 'measurement' only to name what a height is. Please confirm the book is happy with 'measurement' as the contrast to 'count'.

I treated 'counts treated as continuous' and 'measurements treated as discrete' as two separate errors (different trigger, different wrong answer, different argument). If a reviewer prefers a single 'swaps discrete and continuous' entry, the two could be merged, but one refutation would then have to argue in both directions.

entries.label: Calls a set of choices anecdotal because people gave them
entries.description: The student sees that the data comes from what learners say about themselves (their provider, their favourite spread) and calls it anecdotal, taking anecdotal to mean 'personal reports' rather than 'in the form of a story'.
entries.signal: Chooses qualitative anecdotal for a list of short answers that repeat, such as network names or sandwich fillings.

refutation.text_md: You are right that this data is qualitative, because it is not made of numbers. The slip is in the next decision: you called it anecdotal, perhaps because the learners are telling us about themselves, and that feels like a personal account.

Who supplied the data does not decide its type. Anecdotal data takes the form of a story. Categorical data comes from a limited set of possibilities. So ask what each response looks like, not where it came from.

Try it on the cellular providers. Each learner answers with one provider name, such as Vodacom or MTN, and the same few names turn up again and again. Nobody tells a story: every answer is one of a small number of possibilities. That is categorical.
The sandwich spreads work the same way. In a list of five answers, cheese appears twice, and every answer is a single item from a limited set of fillings. Again categorical, not anecdotal.

Once you have decided the data is qualitative, ask: does each response tell a story, or is it one of a limited set of possibilities? Short answers that repeat from a small set are categorical; stories are anecdotal.

entries.label: Calls sentences categorical because they are words
entries.description: The student correctly sees that the data is not numbers, then calls it categorical when each response is a whole sentence in the learner's own words, as if any words count as categories.
entries.signal: Chooses qualitative categorical for a data set made of full sentences or statements.

refutation.text_md: You are right that this data is qualitative, since it cannot be written as numbers. The slip is treating all word data as categorical, as if being written in words were enough to make something a category.
Categorical data comes from a limited set of possibilities: you could list the choices in advance, and every answer would be one of them. Cheese, peanut butter, jam and honey work that way.

Now look at three learners' dreams: "I want to build a bridge!", "I want to help the sick." and "I want running water!". Each learner has said something in their own words. There is no short list these answers were picked from.
That is why this data set is anecdotal: it takes the form of a story, with each learner telling their dream their own way. So it is qualitative anecdotal, not qualitative categorical.
When data is qualitative, ask: could these responses have been picked from a short list, or does each learner say it in their own words? A short list means categorical; own words means anecdotal.

entries.label: Says 'qualitative' and stops
entries.description: The student sees that the data is descriptive rather than numerical and calls it qualitative, but does not say whether it is categorical or anecdotal, or why.
entries.signal: The final answer is only 'qualitative' (or 'descriptive, not numerical') with no categorical or anecdotal and no reason.

refutation.text_md: You are half way there. You spotted that the data is descriptive and not numerical, and that is exactly what makes it qualitative. But categorising the data set takes two decisions, and 'qualitative' is only the first.

The word qualitative fits both a list of sandwich spreads (cheese, jam, honey) and a list of learners' dreams such as "I want to help the sick." Yet these are different kinds of data. The spreads come from a limited set of possibilities, so they are categorical. The dreams take the form of a story, so they are anecdotal.
An answer that only says 'qualitative' cannot tell those two data sets apart, so it does not yet describe either one. The second decision, categorical or anecdotal, is what finishes the job.

Give both parts in one sentence, with the reason for each. For example: 'This data cannot be written as numbers, so it is qualitative; it comes from a limited set of possibilities, so it is categorical.' For a story-like data set, swap the second part for 'it takes the form of a story, so it is anecdotal'.

entries.label: Calls data made of words quantitative
entries.description: The student chooses quantitative (discrete or continuous) for a data set whose responses are names, items or sentences, without checking whether the data can be written as numbers.
entries.signal: Chooses quantitative discrete or quantitative continuous for a list of names, items or sentences.

refutation.text_md: You treated this data as numerical. That is an understandable first guess, because there are numbers around the data, such as how many learners were asked. But the question is about what the responses themselves are.

The book's test is whether the data set can be written as numbers. Take the cellular providers: a learner's response is Vodacom, MTN or Cell C. None of these is a number, so quantitative cannot be right, whichever of discrete or continuous you picked.

The same holds for the sandwich spreads (cheese, peanut butter, jam, honey) and for learners' dreams written as sentences. Responses that are names, items or sentences cannot be written as numbers, so these data sets are qualitative.

Before you choose, read each response and ask: is this a number? If it is a name, an item or a sentence, the data is qualitative, and your next job is to decide whether it is categorical or anecdotal.

No source says why a student would pick each option, so the 'perhaps because' diagnoses in step 1 are inferences, not documented student behaviour.

I used 'limited set of possibilities' as the main phrase and 'small number of possibilities' once for the providers. Please confirm this is acceptable.

The book's reason for calling the dreams anecdotal is that the data 'takes the form of a story'. I followed that wording even though one-line statements are a thin kind of story. 'In their own words' is my paraphrase, not a book term.

Discrete and continuous appear only as option labels and are not defined or taught anywhere in this objective's questions. The 'quantitative-for-words' entry therefore does not distinguish them and uses only the book's 'cannot be written as numbers' test.

The cellular-provider data in the extracted question text is garbled: the entries run together and contain a stray fragment ('8-ta', probably a provider name). I could not use the exact list or counts, so the text names only Vodacom, MTN and Cell C and states no totals. The spreads solution also ends in a stray 'para>' extraction artefact.

No new entries were written, because no evidence was supplied. The evidence section said (none): no caution box, no worked-example remark, no wrong turn from the independent re-solve, and no wrong options or widget predicates (no D0, D1, ...). The task allows an entry only where the evidence supports it, and the runtime falls back to the canonical solution when an objective has no entry, so I did not invent one.

Candidate errors for a human reviewer to consider if the team wants entries here. Each is built into the book's own method but has no evidence that students actually make it. (1) Taking the middle value without sorting first. The worked example with seven unsorted values gives 2 if you take the fourth value as listed, against the book's 14. (2) For an even number of values, picking one of the two middle values instead of averaging them. The worked example with eight values gives 12.5, and two middle values of 13 and 13 give 13. The stem of the question about p+1, p+2, p+9 says 'Five data values' but lists only three, and the canonical solution divides by 3 and gets p + 4. A student who divides by 5 would be following the stem as printed. This looks like a stem defect, not a student error, so I did not turn it into an entry. It needs human review of the stem.

The canonical sorted list for the question on the ages of Ndeme's class's learners shows 9 values (4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7). The original data has 10 values, and the sorted list is missing one 6. The mode of 6 is still correct. This was not used as evidence of a student error.

Two canonical solutions use content outside this objective's description. The pulse-rate question also asks for the range. The golden-ratio digits question finds its median with a percentile-position formula (r_50 = 10.5). That formula is not the 'halfway between the two middle values' rule the other solutions use. Neither was used. Any entry about the even-count median should argue only from the halfway rule.

The book's terms in these solutions are 'mean', 'median', 'mode', 'modal age', 'data set', 'measure of central tendency', 'no mode' and 'two modes'. 'Bimodal' and 'average' are not used. I did not rely on any term outside this set.

entries.label: Gives a mode for continuous measurements
entries.description: The student picks the mass that repeats in a day's bread data and reports it as the mode, instead of saying that a mode usually cannot be computed for continuous data.
entries.signal: A particular mass written as the mode of a day's bread masses, for example 789.0 g for Monday, or a table with a mode column filled in.

refutation.text_md: You looked for the value that appears most often and called it the mode. That is what a mode is, so your method is sound. The problem is the kind of data you are applying it to.

Bread masses are continuous: a mass can be any real number, not just a few fixed values. When measurements can fall anywhere, two loaves matching exactly is usually a coincidence rather than a pattern, so a repeated value does not tell you which mass is typical. This is why the book says we can usually not compute the mode of a continuous data set.

Here is what goes wrong in practice. Among Monday's ten masses, $789.0\ \text{g}$ appears twice, so you might call it the mode. But it is the lightest mass of the day, well below Monday's mean of $800.8\ \text{g}$ and median of $801.8\ \text{g}$. Two loaves happening to match tells you nothing about where the typical loaf sits.

So for continuous data like these, do not report a mode. Write that the data are continuous, so the mode cannot be computed. Then work out the mean (add the ten masses and divide by $10$) and the median (sort the masses and take the value halfway between the two middle ones), and use those two to judge whether the loaves meet the requirement.

entries.label: Expects the mean and median to agree
entries.description: The student expects the mean and median to come out the same or nearly the same, so a gap between them is taken as an arithmetic slip, or only one of the two is worked out and the other is assumed to match.

refutation.text_md: You expected the mean and the median to match, so when they differ you suspect you made a mistake, or you work out only one and assume the other would agree. That is a fair expectation for the bread data, because the two are close there. But close is not the same as equal.

The two measures find the centre in different ways. The mean adds all ten masses and divides by $10$, so every value counts by its size. The median sorts the masses and takes the value in the middle; with $10$ masses that is halfway between the two middle numbers. Two different methods will seldom give exactly the same number.

The results for the seven days show this. Thursday has a mean of $803.4\ \text{g}$ and a median of $800.8\ \text{g}$. Friday has a mean of $802.0\ \text{g}$ and a median of $804.3\ \text{g}$. On none of the seven days are the mean and median equal, and nothing has gone wrong. The book also warns that the mean and median are not always close to each other, so a difference is not a sign of an error, and one measure cannot stand in for the other.

So work out both and set them side by side. Then compare them with the requirement. For the bread, $800\ \text{g}$ with $5$ percent under and $10$ percent over gives limits of $760\ \text{g}$ and $880\ \text{g}$. Both the mean and the median sit close to $800\ \text{g}$ on every day, and every individual measurement is inside the limits, so the supplier is reliable.

flags.text: No wrong options, widget predicates, existing entries or re-solve wrong turns were supplied. The only evidence is the two printed cautions (the mode of continuous data; the mean and median not always being close), so only two entries are written. I did not write an entry for misreading the 5 percent under / 10 percent over leeway, because nothing supplied supports it.

The canonical solution for the motorbike choice (the question about which bike to choose, taking the accuracy of the numbers into account) says bike 1 looks better on the mean and that rounding bike 1's mean to 1 decimal place gives 0.9 s. From the printed times I get roughly 1.02 s for bike 1 and 0.98 s for bike 2, so I could not reproduce those figures. I wrote no entry against that question and recommend a human check of that canonical solution.

The canonical solution for the motorbike measure-of-centre question recommends the mean and the mode, because bike 2's times repeat. That is why the mode entry is worded 'usually' and tied to the bread masses, and says nothing against the mode in general. I also wrote no entry for choosing the median there, since the book's reason for rejecting it is only one sentence and no error evidence was supplied.

In the bread worked example, the sorted Monday list printed in the canonical solution shows 796.7, 802.3 and 808.7, but the raw Monday column of the data table gives 796.8, 802.4 and 808.8. The printed mean (800.8 g), median (801.8 g) and sum (8007.9) are consistent with the raw data. In the refutation I used only the fact that 789.0 g appears twice and is Monday's lightest mass, which holds in both lists.

I used the book's words 'continuous', 'mean', 'median', 'mode' and 'leeway' (the last only implicitly, through the 5 percent and 10 percent limits). I did not use 'measure of central tendency' in student-facing text, though the book uses it in the motorbike question. I used 'limits' for the 760 g and 880 g bounds, where the book says 'range'. A reviewer may want the book's word there.

The only evidence supplied is the worked-example remark on p.363 (WE8), which says outliers are common in experiments because of equipment problems or unexpected interference. That states why outliers occur. It does not describe a mistake students make, so it supports no refutation. No wrong options, no widget predicates and no re-solve wrong turns were supplied for this objective, so no entry was written and the runtime falls back to the canonical solution.

Two errors are plausible for this objective but have no evidence behind them, so they were left out. One is keeping the 'average the two middle values' rule after the count goes from 10 to 11, when the book takes the sixth value. The other is reversing which measure is less affected by the outlier. entries.label: Puts the mode in the set, but not as the most frequent value
entries.description: The student builds a data set with the right mean and median but includes the stated mode only once, or lets two other values repeat as often as it does, as if being in the set were enough to make a value the mode.
entries.signal: A proposed data set in which the stated mode appears only once, or in which another value occurs as many times as the stated mode does.

refutation.text_md: Putting the age $2$ into your set is the right start, and your set may well have the right mean and median. But the mode is not just an age that appears in the set. It is the age that occurs most often.

Try a set with a single $2$, such as $\{1, 2, 3, 8, 11\}$. Its total is $1+2+3+8+11=25$, so the mean is $\frac{25}{5}=5$, and the middle value is $3$. But every age appears once, so nothing makes $2$ the age that occurs most often. The mode is not $2$.

The median is $3$, so $3$ sits in the third position of the ordered set. Every age after it is $3$ or more, so the only positions left for a $2$ are the first two. One $2$ is not enough for the mode to be $2$, so both of those positions must be $2$.
Take care with the last two ages as well. If $x_4$ and $x_5$ were the same age, that age would also occur twice, and then the mode would not be $2$.

So write the mode in twice: $\{2, 2, 3, x_4, x_5\}$. The mean then gives $2+2+3+x_4+x_5=25$, so $x_4+x_5=18$. Choose two different ages that add to $18$, for example $4$ and $14$, which gives $\{2, 2, 3, 4, 14\}$.

entries.label: Finds the median in the list as written, not in the ordered set
entries.description: The student takes the middle of the values in the order they are listed, or places the median value in the middle of an unordered list, instead of putting the data in order first.

refutation.text_md: Going to the middle of the data is the right idea, because the median is a middle value. The catch is that the middle must be found in the ordered data set, from smallest to largest, not in the order the values happen to be written.

Take the list $3;8;8;5;9;1;4;x$ with a median of $6$. Written like this, the fourth and fifth values are $5$ and $9$, which would give a median of $7$ whatever $x$ is. That number has no link to $x$, so it cannot help you find $x$.
Order the values first. Without $x$ they are $\{1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 8, 9\}$. With $x$ there are $8$ values, so the median lies between the fourth and fifth values of the ordered set.

If $x$ is the fourth or fifth value, the middle two values are $5$ and $x$, so $6=\frac{5+x}{2}$, which gives $x=7$. If $x$ were anywhere else in the ordered set, the median would be $\frac{5+8}{2}=6.5$, not $6$.
Before you use a median, write the values in order, count them to find the middle position or positions, and only then place the unknown value.

flags.text: The evidence block was empty and no wrong options or widget predicates were supplied. Both entries rest only on remarks printed inside the worked example's own solution (the parenthetical reminder to use the ordered data set, the note that one 2 would not make the mode 2, the note that equal x4 and x5 would not give a mode of 2, and the closing note that the set must be ordered with two ages of 2) plus the median-case working in the median = 6 question. Drop either entry if a stricter reading of 'evidence' is wanted; neither is padded beyond that text.

Nothing in the evidence or the solutions supports them, so they are left to the canonical-solution fallback.

The set {1, 2, 3, 8, 11} in the mode entry is my own illustration, not a data set printed in the book (total 25, mean 5, median 3, every age occurring once). The 'fourth and fifth values as written are 5 and 9, giving 7' point in the ordering entry is derived from the list as printed. Please check both. The data set {2, 2, 3, 4, 14} is the book's own first data set.

entries.label: Puts a value that sits on the edge of a range into the wrong range
entries.description: The student places a data value that equals the end of a range into whichever neighbouring range feels right, instead of letting the inequality signs decide, so the counts (and the bar heights) are off by the number of such values.

refutation.text_md: Grouping and counting is the right plan. The slip is with a value that sits exactly on the end of a range, like a learner who is exactly $140$ cm tall: it can look as if it fits in two neighbouring ranges, so it gets put in the one that feels right.

The ranges do not overlap because each one starts where the previous one ended, so every value belongs to exactly one range. The inequality signs decide which one. In $130\le h<140$ the top end uses $<$, so $140$ is not allowed in. In $140\le h<150$ the bottom end uses $\le$, so $140$ is allowed in. A height of $140$ goes in the second range.

Check it with real numbers. In the list of $30$ heights, exactly one learner is $140$ cm tall. With that learner in $140\le h<150$, the counts for the first two ranges are $7$ and $5$. Putting $140$ in the first range would give $8$ and $4$, which moves one learner into the wrong bar.

The signs can sit on the other end, so read them each time. With the ranges $20<x\le30$ and $30<x\le40$, the $\le$ is on the upper end, so a guess of exactly $30$ goes in the lower range. Two guesses were exactly $30$, which is why $20<x\le30$ has $13$ and $30<x\le40$ has $15$. Putting them in the upper range would give $11$ and $17$.
When a range is written with $\le$ at both ends, such as $0\le\text{number of playing cards}\le3$, both end values count. A learner with exactly $3$ cards is in that range.

Next time, when a value sits exactly on the end of a range, look at the signs of the two ranges that meet there. Only one of them has $\le$ at that end, and that range gets the value. Then add up your counts: every value is in exactly one range, so they must add up to the number of values you started with.

flags.text: The evidence block was empty: no caution box, no re-solve wrong turn, and no wrong options or widget predicates. The one entry rests only on the book's own parenthetical in the heights worked example (the ranges do not overlap because each starts where the previous one ended) and on the boundary values in the book's worked counts. If you want an entry only where a caution, a re-solve wrong turn or a deliberate wrong option exists, drop it; the runtime then falls back to the canonical solutions.

The book's own words are used: range, grouped frequency table, histogram, count, frequency. The book does not name the edge of a range, so I wrote 'the end of a range' and 'where the previous one ended' (the book's phrase) and avoided 'boundary', 'class' and 'bin'.

The book uses two conventions: the heights example puts the closed end at the bottom ($130\le h<140$), and the sweets and traffic-survey examples put it at the top ($10<x\le20$). Step 4 relies on the student reading the signs each time, not on a single rule.

Not used: the axis of the heights histogram figure is labelled 'Height (m)' while the data are in centimetres. That is a figure-label discrepancy, not a student error, and it is not mentioned in any refutation step.

entries.label: Reads a tall column as big numbers
entries.description: The student takes the height of a column to say how large the values in that range are, instead of how many values fall in that range.

refutation.text_md: You are reading a tall column as meaning big numbers. That is a natural first guess, and you are right that the height tells you something about the values in that range. What it tells you is how many values are there, not how big they are.

The numbers under the columns, like $12$–$15$, say which values a range covers. The height of the column says how many of the values in the data set land in that range. A tall column is the range where most of the values are, whether those values are small or large.

For example, with $15$ learners counting their stones, a column over $12$–$15$ that is $6$ high means six learners have between $12$ and $15$ stones. It does not say that any of them has $6$ stones. All the column heights together add up to $15$, the number of learners, because each learner's value lands in exactly one column.
To count the values in a range, find its column and read its height. That number is your count.

entries.label: Puts a number at the edge of a range into the neighbouring range
entries.description: The student sorts a value that sits at the edge of a range, such as a $4$ in ranges $0$–$3$ and $4$–$7$, into the next or previous range, so one column is counted one too many and its neighbour one too few.

refutation.text_md: You may have put a number that sits at the edge of a range into its neighbour, for example a $4$ into the range $0$–$3$. Going range by range through the sorted list is the right plan. The slip is only in where the edge numbers go.
Each range includes both numbers in its label, so $4$–$7$ holds $4$, $5$, $6$ and $7$. The next range starts at the very next whole number, so every whole number belongs to exactly one range.

Say the sorted values of a group of learners begin $1, 4, 6, 6, 6, 6, 8$, and the ranges are $0$–$3$ and $4$–$7$. The range $0$–$3$ has just the $1$, so its count is $1$. The range $4$–$7$ has the $4$ and the four $6$s, so its count is $5$. Slip the $4$ into $0$–$3$ and you would count $2$ and $4$ instead, and both columns would come out wrong.
To count a range, first write out the whole numbers it covers, for example $4, 5, 6, 7$. Then count every value in the sorted list that is one of those numbers. The edge numbers count.

stripped.reason: no named error: A column letter records which column was ticked, not why. Ticking a correctly drawn column only shows the student's count for that range differed from the right one, and many slips cause that.
no named error: Same as D0: a correctly drawn column ticked, with no single named error behind the choice.

entries.label: Expects the grouped mean to be the exact mean
entries.description: The student treats the answer from grouped data as the true mean of the original values, or is puzzled that it can differ from the mean of the individual values.

refutation.text_md: Your working can be spot on and still not give the exact mean, and that is fine. The number you get from grouped data is an **estimate** of the mean, not the exact mean of the original values.

Grouping loses information. Once a value is placed in a range, all we know is that it lies somewhere in that range. In the taxi data, 16 weeks had between $700$ and $800$ passengers. One of those weeks could be $701$, another $799$, and the groups cannot tell us which.

So the method treats every value in a group as lying at the centre of its range: all 16 of those weeks are counted as $750$. The book makes the same point: with grouped data the estimates of the centre change, because some information is lost.
Use the method as it stands. Multiply each group's centre by its count, add these up, and divide by the total count: $\frac{33600}{48}=700$. Then call it what it is, an estimate of the mean.

entries.label: Looks for one most-common value instead of the modal group
entries.description: The student expects the mode to be a single most common value, as with ungrouped data, and is unsure why the answer for grouped data is a range.

refutation.text_md: Looking for what occurs most often is the right idea for a mode. What changes with grouped data is what you are given: a count for each range, not the individual values.

Because the values have been placed in ranges, you cannot see which single number occurs most often. That information is gone. What the table or histogram does show is how many values fall in each range.

That is why we ask for the **modal group**: the group with the highest number of data values. The book notes that the grouped mode can be a better estimate of the mode than a single most common value, because the grouping shows the range in which the values are clustered.

In the taxi data the groups hold $4$, $6$, $12$, $16$, $8$ and $2$ values. The highest count is $16$, in the group $700<x\leq800$. The $16$ only tells you how many values lie in that group, so the modal group is the range itself.
To find a modal group: compare the counts, pick the largest, and write down the range it belongs to.

entries.label: Picks the median group by counting groups, not values
entries.description: The student takes the middle group in the list of groups as the median group, instead of finding the group that holds the middle data value.
entries.signal: A median group or median estimate taken from the middle of the list of groups, for example $650$ (the centre of the third of six groups) for the passenger data, where the answer is $750$.

refutation.text_md: Looking for the middle group is a reasonable first move, because the median is the middle. The catch is that the median is the middle **data value**, and groups hold different numbers of values. Counting along the list of groups only tells you where the middle of the list is.

In the taxi data there are six groups, holding $4$, $6$, $12$, $16$, $8$ and $2$ values. Six groups have no single middle group. The middle of the list falls between the third and the fourth. If you take the third group you end up with its centre, $650$.
Count values instead. There are $48$ values, so the median lies between the $24^{\text{th}}$ and $25^{\text{th}}$ values.

The first three groups hold $4+6+12=22$ values, so the $23^{\text{rd}}$ value is where the fourth group begins. The first four groups hold $22+16=38$ values. So both the $24^{\text{th}}$ and $25^{\text{th}}$ values are in the fourth group, $700<x\leq800$. That is the median group, and the estimate of the median is the centre of that group, $750$, not $650$.

To find a median group: add up all the counts, find the position of the middle value, then add the group counts one at a time until you reach that position. The group where you get there is the median group.

entries.label: Expects removing one value to leave the range unchanged
entries.description: When asked what happens to the range if the smallest or largest value is removed, or when a value that is not typical of the rest is present, the student expects the range to stay the same or hardly change, forgetting that the range is built only from the largest and the smallest values.
entries.signal: After the smallest value has been removed, the student gives the original range again as the new range (for the worked set, 9 instead of 6), or says the range stays the same.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to think that taking away one number out of many should hardly change anything, and you are right that all the other values stay exactly as they were. The catch is that the range does not use all the values: it uses only the largest and the smallest.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. In the set $\{1, 4, 5, 8, 6, 7, 5, 6, 7, 4, 10, 9, 10\}$ the smallest value is $1$ and the largest value is $10$, so the range is $10-1=9$.

Now take the $1$ away. The smallest value left is $4$, so the range becomes $10-4=6$. Only one number was removed, yet the range dropped from $9$ to $6$, because the number removed was one of the two numbers the range is made from.
The book calls a value that is not typical of the other values an outlier, and the $1$ here is one. An outlier has a big influence on the range: the range is very sensitive to outliers.
So when you are asked what happens if a value is removed, cross it out, find the smallest and the largest values that are left, and subtract again. Here that gives $10-4=6$.

entries.label: Counts to the rank in the list as given, without sorting first
entries.description: The student works out the rank with the percentile formula but counts along the data in the order it was printed, instead of first sorting the values from smallest to largest.
entries.signal: Each answer is built from values at the right positions of the list as it was printed, so for a data set that is not already in order the median and quartiles come out wrong. For the twelve-value data set 3, 5, 1, 8, 9, 12, 25, 28, 24, 30, 41, 50 this gives 4.5, 18.5 and 27 instead of 6.5, 18 and 29.

refutation.text_md: You worked out the rank correctly and then counted to that position, which is the right instinct. The slip is that a rank is a position in the data set **after it has been sorted** from smallest to largest, and the list you are given is usually in no particular order.

Take $\{3, 5, 1, 8, 9, 12, 25, 28, 24, 30, 41, 50\}$. The rank of the lower quartile is $r=\frac{25}{100}(12-1)+1=3.75$, so it lies between the third and fourth values. Counting along the list as printed, those are $1$ and $8$, which gives $\frac{1+8}{2}=4.5$. But $1$ is the smallest number in the whole set, so it cannot be the third smallest.

The percentile formula only makes sense in sorted order. It gives rank $1$ for the minimum (the $0^{\text{th}}$ percentile) and rank $n$ for the maximum (the $100^{\text{th}}$ percentile). Those ranks only point to the smallest and largest values when the values are in order.

Sort first: $\{1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 24, 25, 28, 30, 41, 50\}$. Now the third and fourth values are $5$ and $8$, and the lower quartile is $\frac{5+8}{2}=6.5$. Same rank, different values, different answer.
Make sorting your first step every time: rewrite the data from smallest to largest, check that you still have all $n$ values, and only then use the percentile formula and count along the sorted list.

entries.label: Rounds a fractional rank to one position instead of going halfway between two values
entries.description: When the rank is not a whole number (such as 3.75 or 9.25), the student rounds it to a whole position and reads off that single value, instead of taking the value halfway between the two values either side of the rank.
entries.signal: The answer for a percentile whose rank is not a whole number is one of the values in the data set itself. For the twelve-value data set 1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 24, 25, 28, 30, 41, 50 the lower and upper quartiles come out as 8 and 28 instead of 6.5 and 29.

refutation.text_md: You found the rank correctly and went to the right part of the list, which is good. What is missing is what a rank like $3.75$ means: a data set has a third value and a fourth value but no value at position $3.75$, so the percentile is not one of the values. It lies somewhere between two of them.

Sorted, the data set is $\{1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 24, 25, 28, 30, 41, 50\}$. The rank $3.75$ lies between the third and fourth values, $5$ and $8$. In this book the percentile is then the value halfway between them: $\frac{5+8}{2}=6.5$. Rounding the rank to $4$ would give the fourth value, $8$, which is not the answer.

The same thing happens with the upper quartile. Its rank is $\frac{75}{100}(12-1)+1=9.25$, between the ninth and tenth values, $28$ and $30$. The answer is $\frac{28+30}{2}=29$, not $28$. The median has rank $6.5$, halfway between the sixth and seventh positions, so it is $\frac{12+24}{2}=18$: with $12$ values there is no single middle value to pick.

The rule to keep: if the rank is a whole number, read off the value at that position. If it is not, name the two whole positions either side of it, read both values from the sorted list, add them and divide by $2$.

entries.label: Takes the line inside the box for an end of the box
entries.description: The student treats the line inside the box as the first or third quartile, instead of seeing that the quartiles are the two ends of the box and the line inside is the median.

refutation.text_md: It looks like you took the number to be a quartile. That is a sensible place to look, because the box is where the quartiles live. The catch is which part of the box: a box has three vertical lines, and they do three different jobs.
The book says the box shows the interquartile range, the distance between $Q_1$ and $Q_3$. So the two ends of the box are the quartiles. The line inside the box is the one that shows the median.

Try it on a plot whose whiskers reach $15$ and $35$ and whose box runs from $22$ to $28$, with a line inside the box at $25$. The two ends of the box give $Q_1 = 22$ and $Q_3 = 28$, and the line inside gives the median, $25$. If the line at $25$ were a quartile, the median would be left with no mark on the plot at all.
Next time, look at where your number sits. If it is on an end of the box, it is a quartile. If it is on the line inside the box, between the two ends, it is the median.

entries.label: Takes the line inside the box for the smallest or largest value
entries.description: The student reads a mark in the middle of the plot as the minimum or the maximum, instead of looking to the ends of the whiskers for those two values.

refutation.text_md: It looks like you took the number to be the smallest or the largest value. The plot does show both of those, so looking for them was a sound idea. The catch is which marks they are.

The book says the lines extending outside the box, the whiskers, show where the minimum and maximum values lie. So the minimum is where the lower whisker stops, and the maximum is where the upper whisker stops.

Test it on a plot whose whiskers reach $15$ and $35$, with a line inside the box at $25$. The plot shows values below $25$, because the lower whisker goes down to $15$, and values above $25$, because the upper whisker goes up to $35$. A minimum has nothing below it and a maximum has nothing above it, so a mark in the middle of the box cannot be either one.

Before you choose minimum or maximum, check that your number sits at the outer end of a whisker. A number on a line inside the box is not at a whisker's end, so look to the box instead: its two ends are the quartiles, and the line inside it is the median.
